questions.question: Why do users add fashion products to their wishlist?
questions.answer: Users mainly add fashion products to their wishlist to wait for a sale, salary, or price drop, park items to buy later on purpose, and save something that caught their eye. These are inferred from save/compare/sale language in comments that mention wishlist or saved items.
evidence: Explicit wishlist/save language in 56 of 36118 corpus comments
wait for a sale, salary, or price drop: seen in wishlist-tagged comments
park items to buy later on purpose: seen in wishlist-tagged comments
save something that caught their eye: seen in wishlist-tagged comments
check hauls or photos before committing: seen in wishlist-tagged comments

questions.question: What prevents wishlisted products from being purchased, and what uncertainties remain after users like an item?
questions.answer: What usually prevents a wishlisted product from being purchased is price, delivery or checkout of a saved item, sale timing, and returns. Even after users have found a product they like, leftover uncertainty is mostly fabric or quality, photos vs real product, and review volume or trust. That doubt is often what keeps a saved item from becoming an order.

questions.question: What role do fit, size, styling, price, reviews, occasion and social validation play?
questions.answer: Fit, size, styling, price, reviews, occasion, and social validation each act as either a reason to save or a reason not to buy yet. Price, sales, and fit usually matter most for whether a saved item gets bought; generic quality talk can be loud without being the main conversion blocker.

questions.question: When do users use the wishlist as genuine purchase intent versus simply as a bookmarking mechanism?
questions.answer: Genuine purchase intent shows up when someone wants the item but gets stuck (about 16.3% of these comments). Bookmarking shows up when they are saving for later or on impulse (about 37.5%). Waiting for a sale (about 15.5%) is still real interest — they plan to buy, just not at today’s price. A negative review is not the same as “I want this but can’t check out yet.”

questions.question: How do these behaviors differ across user segments?
questions.answer: Wishlist hesitation is not one behavior — it splits by shopper type, not by phone or app version. We only name a segment when shoppers use explicit cues (sale wait, salary talk, wedding mention, etc.); shares below count comments with that cue, not every wishlist user. Price-first savers (Deal hunters / sale shoppers and Budget / salary-cycle shoppers — about 11.2% of these comments): the list works like a deal tracker. They plan to buy, but only after EORS, a price drop, or payday — the delay is timing or price, not loss of interest. Loyal repeat shoppers (9.4%): they already order on Myntra but still park items. Being a regular customer does not mean saved items convert quickly. Still-building-trust shoppers (First-time shoppers — about 3.4%): new or cautious buyers save while they learn fit, quality, and whether products match photos. The wishlist is a shortlist for research, not a committed buy list. Occasion-led shoppers (Office / workwear shoppers and Wedding / occasion shoppers — about 3.4%): they save outfits for weddings, office, or festivals and pause until the look fits the moment — styling confidence gates the buy more than price. Gen Z, wedding, and festive cues are thinner in public wishlist talk (Office / workwear shoppers, Budget / salary-cycle shoppers, and Wedding / occasion shoppers); treat those shares as directional and validate with survey quotas.
evidence: Deal hunters / sale shoppers: 9.7% (n=26)
Repeat / loyal shoppers: 9.4% (n=25)
First-time shoppers: 3.4% (n=9)
Office / workwear shoppers: 1.9% (n=5)
Budget / salary-cycle shoppers: 1.5% (n=4)
Wedding / occasion shoppers: 1.5% (n=4)

questions.question: What unmet needs emerge consistently across user conversations?
questions.answer: Across user conversations, the unmet needs that emerge most consistently are gaps shoppers still need filled after they save an item — not restating the delay reasons themselves. The strongest repeating needs are: a price they feel is fair enough to buy the saved item now, clear alerts when a saved item’s price drops or a sale starts, timely sale / price-drop help so saved items don’t sit until a sale, and proof the product looks like the photos or haul videos. These are what people are missing before a wishlisted product turns into a purchase.
evidence: a price they feel is fair enough to buy the saved item now: 38.6%
clear alerts when a saved item’s price drops or a sale starts: 11.7%
timely sale / price-drop help so saved items don’t sit until a sale: 9.0%
proof the product looks like the photos or haul videos: 7.4%
Often mentioned, weaker as a wishlist unmet need: hesitate on a saved item because fabric or quality feels uncertain before they commit to a saved item (mentioned #4, conversion rank #12)
